facts.claim: Google’s Site Reliability Engineering book (Mike Ulrich, 2016) says overload is the most common cause of failures that spread: in its example, servers handling 1,000 requests a second that get 1,200 start crashing, and answer well below 1,000.

Cloudflare’s engineers wrote (June 2017) that a count reset at the start of each period lets regular spikes through; their fix, which also weighs the last period’s count, wrongly let through or refused 0.003% of 400 million requests from 270,000 senders (vendor-reported).
RFC 6585 (April 2012) says status 429 Too Many Requests means the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, and the reply may include a Retry-After header saying how long to wait.

RFC 9110 (June 2022), the HTTP standard, says a server sends Retry-After to say how long the client ought to wait before its next request, as a date or a number of seconds; “Retry-After: 120” means 2 minutes.

Amazon API Gateway’s guide says it limits requests with the token bucket method, a token per request: the rate is how fast tokens are added and the burst is the bucket’s size; past both, clients get 429 Too Many Requests.

Amazon API Gateway’s quotas page, checked 30 October 2026, gives each account in a Region 10,000 requests a second, with a bucket of 5,000 for bursts (2,500 and 1,250 in some newer Regions); AWS sets the bucket from the rate.
GitHub’s REST API docs, checked 30 October 2026, give each signed-in user their own limit of 5,000 requests an hour, and 60 an hour per address for requests without a sign-in.
The same GitHub docs say that when a limited reply carries retry-after, a client should not retry until that many seconds have passed, and that clients which keep sending while limited may be banned.

Marc Brooker (AWS Architecture Blog, 2015) found that backoff alone still leaves retries in clusters, and that adding jitter spreads them out and, with 100 clients competing in his simulation, more than halves the calls.
